opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so RLACE, Relaxed Linear Adversarial Concept Erasure from Shauli Ravfogel and colleagues, was an important step, and LEACE was partly a response to it.

The basic idea of RLACE is to set up a minimax game. You have a linear classifier trying to predict some concept, say gender or part of speech, from the representations, and you have an orthogonal projection trying to remove that information. You optimize the projection to make the best classifier do as badly as possible. It's a nice framing, and it works reasonably well in practice.

My issues with it are mostly about guarantees and efficiency. First, it's an iterative adversarial optimization. Minimax problems like that are finicky. You don't know you've reached a global solution, and it's computationally expensive, especially in high dimensions or when you want to erase at every layer of a large model.

Second, and more fundamentally, it doesn't guarantee that linear information is gone. You've beaten the classifiers your optimization happened to find. That doesn't prove no linear classifier can still extract the concept. If what you care about is a guarantee, like for fairness auditing or interpretability experiments where you're doing causal interventions, that's a meaningful gap.

Third, RLACE isn't really trying to be minimal. It removes a rank-k subspace, but it isn't explicitly optimizing to change the representations as little as possible. So you can get collateral damage, wiping out other useful information along with the concept.

With LEACE, we showed you can get a closed-form solution. The key result is that a concept is linearly guarded, meaning no linear classifier can beat a constant predictor, if and only if the class-conditional means are all equal, or equivalently the cross-covariance between the representation and the concept label is zero. Once you know that's the condition, you can find the affine transformation that achieves it while minimizing the expected squared distance from the original representations. You compute it from covariance statistics. There's no adversarial training, it's fast, and it's provably optimal for the objective.

So I'd say RLACE got the problem framing right and had a lot of influence. But if you want guaranteed linear erasure with minimal side effects, I think a closed-form approach dominates it. The caveat for both methods is that they only address linear information. A nonlinear probe can often still recover the concept, so you shouldn't oversell what "erasure" means.

r001.rationale: It describes a minimax game where a linear classifier predicts the concept and the projection is optimized to make the best classifier perform worse.

r002.rationale: It calls the optimization finicky and notes uncertainty about reaching a global solution, but does not identify cycling as a possible cause of nonconvergence.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so RLACE — Relaxed Linear Adversarial Concept Erasure — is Ravfogel and colleagues' method, and I think it's a genuinely important piece of work, because it was one of the first to take the problem seriously as an adversarial one. The older approaches like INLP would iteratively train a linear probe, project out the direction it found, train another probe, and so on. The problem is that's greedy, and there's no guarantee you end up with a subspace that actually makes the concept linearly unrecoverable. You can run it for many iterations, destroy a lot of information, and still have residual linear leakage.

RLACE reframes it as a minimax game. You have an adversary trying to predict the concept with a linear classifier, and you're searching for an orthogonal projection that maximizes that adversary's loss. The "relaxed" part is that they relax the projection matrix to a continuous set so you can do gradient-based optimization. And empirically it works quite well — you can often remove a concept like gender with a rank-one or very low-rank projection, which is a nice result in itself, because it tells you how much of the linearly accessible information really lives in a small subspace.

My main criticisms are, first, it's an iterative optimization with no closed-form solution and no formal guarantee. It can be slow, it can be finicky, and when it converges you don't have a proof that every linear classifier has been defeated — you have evidence that the particular adversary you trained has been. Second, and this was really the motivation for our LEACE work, the objective is tied to a specific loss. RLACE is optimizing against cross-entropy for a logistic regression adversary. What we showed is that if you want to guarantee that no linear classifier can do better than a constant predictor, for any convex loss, the necessary and sufficient condition is actually very simple: the class-conditional means have to be equal after your transformation. Once you see that, you can derive the optimal edit in closed form — it's basically a whitening, a projection, and an un-whitening — and it's provably the least disruptive affine transformation that achieves linear guardedness. So you get in one shot what RLACE is approximating through optimization, plus a guarantee RLACE doesn't give you.

The other thing I'd flag applies to RLACE, LEACE, all of these: they're linear methods, and they target linear availability of the concept. That is a meaningful notion — if the concept isn't linearly decodable, the next layer can't trivially use it — but it is not the same as the information being gone. A nonlinear probe might still recover it. So I'd assess RLACE as a strong, important step in the lineage, the thing that made the adversarial framing standard, but ultimately superseded by approaches that give you the same linear guarantee analytically, and with the same fundamental ceiling on what "erasure" means.

r001.rationale: It describes a minimax game with a linear classifier predicting the concept and an orthogonal projection maximizing the classifier’s loss, conveying the opposing optimization objectives.

r002.rationale: It says the optimization can be slow and finicky, but does not identify cycling as a possible reason it may fail to converge.

astra-6.text:
I think RLACE is interesting, but you have to be precise about what “removing concept information” means. It looks for a projection that makes a concept difficult for a linear classifier to predict, while an adversarial classifier tries to recover it. So it’s targeting linear decodability, which is a narrower claim than saying the representation contains no information about the concept.

A nonlinear decoder might still recover that information. And if you apply the projection inside a network, subsequent layers may reconstruct it from other features. There’s also the question of collateral damage: information about the concept can overlap with information you need for the task.

So I’d treat it as a useful intervention, but I wouldn’t equate success against a linear probe with erasing the concept. You also want to test what happens to the model’s behavior, whether stronger probes can recover the information, and how much unrelated performance you lose.

r001.rationale: The response describes a projection and an adversarial classifier, but does not specify an orthogonal projection or explain the opposing minimization and maximization of the same prediction loss.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention cycling or identify it as a possible cause of non-convergence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think RLACE is a useful method, but you have to be precise about what “removing concept information” means. It tries to find a projection of the representation that makes the concept difficult for a linear classifier to predict, using an adversarial optimization procedure. That’s a meaningful objective, but it’s narrower than making the representation independent of the concept.

You could still have information that a nonlinear classifier can recover. And if the rest of your model is nonlinear, that distinction matters: failing to decode something linearly doesn’t establish that the model can’t use it.

There’s also the question of what else you remove. Concepts are correlated with other features, so making one harder to predict can damage information you wanted to preserve. I’d evaluate both concept predictability and performance on the tasks you care about.

So I’d treat RLACE as a tool for studying and suppressing linear accessibility, rather than a guarantee that you’ve deleted a concept or eliminated its influence on the model’s behavior.

r001.rationale: It describes a projection that makes a linear classifier’s prediction difficult through adversarial optimization, but does not explain the minimax game or specify that the classifier minimizes and the orthogonal projection maximizes the same prediction loss.

r002.rationale: It does not mention cycling as a possible cause of nonconvergence.
